question: Which of the following best explains why proton pump inhibitors achieve greater acid suppression than H₂-receptor antagonists?

answers.text: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, the final common pathway of acid secretion regardless of stimulus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. PPIs covalently bind and irreversibly inactivate the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the luminal surface of parietal cells, blocking acid secretion stimulated by histamine, gastrin, and acetylcholine simultaneously.

answers.text: PPIs block all three gastric acid stimulants — histamine, gastrin, and acetylcholine — at their respective receptors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PPIs do not act at receptor level. They act downstream at the proton pump itself, not at the histamine H₂, gastrin (CCK-B), or muscarinic receptors.

answers.text: H₂-receptor antagonists are partial agonists, whereas PPIs are full antagonists at the same receptor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. H₂ antagonists and PPIs act at entirely different molecular targets. H₂ antagonists competitively block histamine receptors; PPIs do not interact with H₂ receptors at all.

answers.text: PPIs have a longer plasma half-life that results in sustained receptor occupancy over 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PPIs actually have a short plasma half-life (~1–2 hours), but their duration of action is long because covalent inactivation of the pump persists until new pump protein is synthesised.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the PPI mechanism section. The key is where in the acid-secretion cascade PPIs act — the proton pump is the final common step, not one of the upstream receptor signals.
Well reasoned. The irreversible covalent binding to H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the defining pharmacological feature of PPIs and the reason they outperform H₂-blockers across all acid-secretory stimuli.
